p.src: Take a photon moving in the $z$-direction with definite momentum and set aside its translational motion. What remains is its transverse polarization. Classically we picture an electric field oscillating along an axis in the $xy$-plane. For a single photon that transverse degree of freedom becomes a particularly clean quantum system: the state space is only two-dimensional, but it already contains superposition, incompatible measurements, complex amplitudes, and probabilistic outcomes.

p.src: The difficulty begins with rotational symmetry. A polarizer can be turned to any angle, so a photon can be prepared along a continuum of linear polarization axes. A fixed analyzer nevertheless has only two outcomes: the photon passes or it does not. No single photon divides into a transmitted fraction and a rejected fraction. Continuous preparations and discrete outcomes must coexist.

p.src:
Represent the two orthogonal states by $\ket{x}=
  \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \ket{y}=
  \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$ They obey $\braket{x}{x}=\braket{y}{y}=1,
  \qquad
  \braket{x}{y}=0.$ These are two basis vectors, not the only two state vectors. Every normalized superposition $\ket{\psi}=a\ket{x}+b\ket{y},
  \qquad
  |a|^2+|b|^2=1,$ is a possible pure polarization state. Multiplication of the entire vector by one common phase does not change the physical state.

p.src:
To turn a test into an observable, attach numbers to its outcomes. Record $+1$ when an $x$-analyzer transmits the photon and $-1$ when it rejects it. The labels are conventional; $7$ and $12$ would distinguish the outcomes too. The symmetric choice $\pm1$ gives $\hat P_0\ket{x}=+\ket{x},
  \qquad
  \hat P_0\ket{y}=-\ket{y},$ and therefore $\hat P_0=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1&0\\
    0&-1
  \end{pmatrix}
  =\ket{x}\bra{x}-\ket{y}\bra{y}.$

p.src: The operator can be constructed from known eigenstates and recorded values, as we have just done. In other problems the order is reversed: one begins with an operator and solves for its eigenvectors and eigenvalues. For example, the wave-number operator $-i\,d/dx$ is given first, and its plane-wave eigenstates are then found. Either route expresses the same postulate: an observable has definite value $\lambda$ in a state satisfying $\hat A\ket{\lambda}=\lambda\ket{\lambda}$.

p.src:
The amplitude that a slash-polarized photon passes an $x$-analyzer is $\braket{x}{d_+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}.$ The probability is the absolute square, $\operatorname{Prob}(x|d_+)
  =|\braket{x}{d_+}|^2=\frac12,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Prob}(y|d_+)=\frac12.$ The amplitude and the probability are not interchangeable. Amplitudes may be negative or complex; probabilities are nonnegative real numbers.

p.src:
Suppose the first polarizer prepares $\ket{\theta}$ and the second tests the $x$-direction. Then $\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Prob}(x|\theta)
  &=|\braket{x}{\theta}|^2
  =\cos^2\theta,\\
  \operatorname{Prob}(y|\theta)&=\sin^2\theta.
  \end{aligned}$ Their sum is one. Reversing the inner product does not change the probability because $\braket{\theta}{x}=\braket{x}{\theta}^{*}$.

p.src:
Prepare $\ket{\theta}$ and test it directly with the orthogonal analyzer $\theta+\pi/2$. The transmission probability vanishes: $\operatorname{Prob}(\theta+\pi/2|\theta)
  =\cos^2(\pi/2)=0.$ Now insert an $x$-polarizer between them. Passing the intermediate polarizer has probability $\cos^2\theta$, and passage prepares the new state $\ket{x}$. Conditional on that event, transmission through the last analyzer has probability $\operatorname{Prob}(\theta+\pi/2|x)
  =\cos^2(\theta+\pi/2)=\sin^2\theta.$ The probability of completing both stages is therefore $\operatorname{Prob}
  (\theta\longrightarrow x\longrightarrow\theta+\pi/2)
  =\cos^2\theta\,\sin^2\theta.$

p.src:
The general analyzer must have $\ket{\theta}$ and $\ket{\theta_\perp}$ as eigenvectors: $\hat P_\theta\ket{\theta}=+\ket{\theta},
  \qquad
  \hat P_\theta\ket{\theta_\perp}=-\ket{\theta_\perp}.$ Its spectral form is already the answer: $\hat P_\theta
  =\ket{\theta}\bra{\theta}
   -\ket{\theta_\perp}\bra{\theta_\perp}.$ In the $x,y$ basis, $\begin{aligned}
  \hat P_\theta
  &=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta&
    2\sin\theta\cos\theta\\
    2\sin\theta\cos\theta&
    \sin^2\theta-\cos^2\theta
  \end{pmatrix}\\
  &=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \cos2\theta&\sin2\theta\\
    \sin2\theta&-\cos2\theta
  \end{pmatrix}.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src:
To see their wave meaning, restore a dimensionally explicit phase $\phi=kz-\omega t$, with $\omega=ck$. Equal in-phase components, $E_x=E_0\cos\phi,
  \qquad
  E_y=E_0\cos\phi,$ make a linearly polarized wave at $45^\circ$. A relative quarter-cycle shift gives $E_x=E_0\sin\phi,
  \qquad
  E_y=E_0\cos\phi.$ At a fixed point in space, the tip of $\bm E=E_x\hat{\bm x}+E_y\hat{\bm y}$ moves around a circle. Reversing the sign of one quadrature reverses the sense of rotation. The magnetic field is transverse as well; in vacuum, $\bm B=\hat{\bm z}\times\bm E/c$.

p.src:
For any linear analyzer, $\braket{\theta}{c_+}
  =\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
    \bigl(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\bigr).$ Hence $\begin{aligned}
  |\braket{\theta}{c_+}|^2
  &=
  \frac12
  (\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)
  (\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)\\
  &=\frac12(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)
  =\frac12.
  \end{aligned}$ A circularly polarized photon therefore passes every linear analyzer with probability one half. Its statistics reveal no preferred linear axis.

p.src:
The axial, diagonal, arbitrary linear, and circular observables do not usually share eigenvectors. In the present two-state space, $\hat P_\theta
  =\cos2\theta\,\sigma_z+\sin2\theta\,\sigma_x,$ so two linear analyzers satisfy $=2i\sin\!\bigl(2(\beta-\alpha)\bigr)\sigma_y.$ They commute only when their axes are the same or orthogonal, modulo the $\pi$-periodicity of a linear polarization axis. In the orthogonal case $\hat P_{\theta+\pi/2}=-\hat P_\theta$, so measuring one immediately fixes the other with the opposite label.

p.src: Incompatibility is therefore not vagueness about an apparatus. Each apparatus is perfectly definite. It is the impossibility of one state being a simultaneous eigenstate of two noncommuting tests.

p.src: Expectation Value Means Average Value

u.src: Expectation Value Means Average Value
en: Expectation Value Means Average Value

p.src: The standard term expectation value can be misleading. Imagine a position probability density concentrated in two symmetric, separated lobes. Its average position is zero, even if the probability of finding the particle near zero is tiny or vanishes. The average need not be a likely single outcome.

p.src:
Let $\hat K$ be a Hermitian observable with a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, $\hat K\ket{n}=\lambda_n\ket{n},
  \qquad
  \sum_n\ket{n}\bra{n}=\mathbf 1.$ For a normalized state $\ket{\psi}$, define $\expect{\hat K}_\psi
  :=\bra{\psi}\hat K\ket{\psi}.$

en:
Let $\hat K$ be a Hermitian observable with a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, $\hat K\ket{n}=\lambda_n\ket{n},
  \qquad
  \sum_n\ket{n}\bra{n}=\mathbf 1.$ For a normalized state $\ket{\psi}$, define $\expect{\hat K}_\psi
  :=\bra{\psi}\hat K\ket{\psi}.$

p.src:
Insert the eigenbasis resolution of identity between $\hat K$ and $\ket{\psi}$: $\begin{aligned}
  \expect{\hat K}_\psi
  &=
  \bra{\psi}\hat K
  \left(\sum_n\ket{n}\bra{n}\right)
  \ket{\psi}\\
  &=
  \sum_n
  \bra{\psi}\hat K\ket{n}
  \braket{n}{\psi}\\
  &=
  \sum_n
  \lambda_n
  \braket{\psi}{n}
  \braket{n}{\psi}\\
  &=
  \sum_n\lambda_n
  |\braket{n}{\psi}|^2.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src: The factor $p_n=|\braket{n}{\psi}|^2$ is the probability of obtaining $\lambda_n$. Thus $\expect{\hat K}_\psi=\sum_n p_n\lambda_n$ is exactly an ordinary weighted average of the possible outcomes.

p.src: The same answer follows directly from the two outcomes: $(+1)\cos^2\theta+(-1)\sin^2\theta=\cos2\theta.$ No single detector click reports $\cos2\theta$. Each run still records $+1$ or $-1$; $\cos2\theta$ emerges only as the average over repeated identically prepared photons. That distinction between a state, a single-shot outcome, a probability, and an ensemble average completes the two-state polarization example.
